source_user: Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Mechanism. Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound: every generated token must re-read all weights from HBM. Time per output token (TPOT) is approximately (weight_bytes + kv_bytes_touched) / effective_HBM_bandwidth, plus kernel launch and communication overhead. Weight-only INT4 (W4A16) on a 9B model drops weight traffic from ~18 GB (BF16) to ~5 GB, so the bandwidth-limited floor of TPOT drops roughly 3-3.5x. On an A30 (933 GB/s HBM2, ~24 GB), the BF16 floor is ~19 ms/token single-stream and the W4A16 floor is ~5-6 ms/token; measured values will be worse because dequantization is done in-kernel and adds ALU work.

Separately, quantization frees capacity: 13 GB of weight savings converts directly into KV-cache blocks, which raises the maximum concurrent sequence count and therefore throughput even if per-token latency were unchanged. FP8 KV cache is a second, independent lever: it halves kv_bytes_touched, which matters at long context where KV traffic exceeds weight traffic.

Boundary condition. The latency win inverts at high arithmetic intensity. In prefill, and in decode at large batch, the GEMM is compute bound, not bandwidth bound; W4A16 then pays dequantization cost on the critical path with no traffic saving to recover it, and can be 10-30% *slower* than a well-tuned BF16 or FP8 tensor-core path. The crossover is where batch * activation_bytes approaches weight_bytes. Concretely: W4A16 is the right choice for low-concurrency, latency-sensitive decode; W8A8/FP8 (which quantizes activations too, so tensor cores run at reduced precision) is the right choice for high-throughput batched serving. On A30 there is no hardware FP8 tensor core (that starts at Hopper/SM90), so FP8 there is emulated or storage-only and the compute-side win does not exist.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: W4A16 reduces p50 TPOT by >=2x at concurrency 1 and by <1.2x at concurrency 64. Gate: reject the quantized build if held-out task accuracy drops more than 1 point absolute, or if p99 TTFT regresses at the target concurrency.
risks: Source answer states no mechanism, no bit width, and no bandwidth model
Does not name the batch-size regime where the latency win disappears or inverts
No numeric accuracy or p99 regression gate
evidence_required: Concurrency sweep (1,4,16,64) of TPOT p50/p99 and tokens/s, BF16 vs W4A16 vs W8A8
ncu or DCGM dram__bytes_read per decode step to confirm traffic reduction
Held-out downstream accuracy, not perplexity alone
GPU arch capability check for FP8 tensor-core support

source_user: Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Mechanism (memory side). Quantization changes three distinct budgets and they must not be conflated. (1) Weight residency: BF16 weights are 2 bytes/param, INT4 with group-128 scales is ~0.53 bytes/param including metadata. For a 9B model that is 18 GB -> ~4.8 GB. (2) KV cache: bytes = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * seq_len per sequence; FP8 KV halves it, INT4 KV quarters it. (3) Activation/workspace, which quantization usually does not shrink and sometimes grows because dequantized tiles are staged in registers or shared memory.

The throughput consequence is indirect but dominant in practice: freed HBM becomes KV blocks, KV blocks become admitted concurrent sequences, and concurrency is what fills the tensor cores during decode. A vLLM-style scheduler reports this as a higher gpu_cache_usage ceiling and fewer preemptions/recomputations. That path often yields a larger throughput gain than the per-token bandwidth saving does.

Boundary condition. Freed memory only converts to throughput while the workload is memory-limited on KV. Once the batch is large enough that decode becomes compute or scheduler bound, adding KV capacity buys nothing and W4A16 dequant overhead becomes pure loss. A second boundary: group-wise INT4 with very small groups (g=32) improves accuracy but inflates scale metadata and shrinks the memory win, while per-tensor INT8 has the smallest metadata but is the most vulnerable to activation outliers in later layers.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: at fixed 24 GB, W4A16 raises the sustainable concurrent-sequence count at 8k context by >=2x and raises aggregate tokens/s by >=1.5x. Gate: roll back if preemption rate rises, if p99 TTFT exceeds SLO, or if accuracy regression exceeds the agreed threshold on a held-out set.
risks: Source conflates weight memory, KV memory, and activation memory into one vague claim
Does not state that freed memory only helps while KV-capacity is the binding constraint
No mention of quantization metadata overhead reducing the nominal saving
evidence_required: Measured HBM breakdown (weights, KV, activations) before and after via torch.cuda.memory_summary or server metrics
Scheduler metrics: cache usage, preemption/recompute counts
Throughput at fixed context length and fixed SLO, not peak tokens/s

source_user: Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Mechanism (kernel side). A quantized linear layer is only fast if a fused kernel exists for that exact (weight dtype, activation dtype, group size, layout) tuple. W4A16 kernels such as Marlin/Machete load INT4 tiles, dequantize in registers, and feed BF16 tensor cores; the dequant is hidden behind the memory fetch only while the layer is bandwidth bound. If no fused kernel matches the checkpoint's scheme, the runtime falls back to dequantize-to-BF16-then-GEMM, which materializes the full-precision weight tile in memory and is strictly slower than never quantizing at all. This is the single most common cause of 'we quantized and got no speedup'.

The latency impact is therefore discontinuous, not smooth: it is a function of kernel availability, not of bit width. Checking which kernel was selected (server logs naming the quant backend, or a Nsight kernel trace showing the fused GEMM name) is a prerequisite to any latency claim.

Boundary condition. Kernel coverage is architecture gated. Marlin-class W4A16 kernels require Ampere (SM80) or newer; FP8 tensor cores require Hopper (SM90) or newer; NVFP4 requires Blackwell. On A30 (SM80) INT4/INT8 tensor-core paths exist but FP8 compute does not, so an FP8 checkpoint runs emulated and shows no throughput gain. A second boundary: tensor-parallel sharding must divide cleanly by the quantization group size, or the runtime silently falls back or refuses to load.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: the fused quantized kernel is selected and per-layer GEMM time drops >=2x at concurrency 1. Gate: if the kernel trace shows a separate dequant kernel, treat the quantized build as failed and do not report a latency number for it.
risks: Source mentions 'kernel support' without explaining that missing kernels make quantization slower, not merely neutral
No architecture gating (SM80 vs SM90 vs SM100) for INT4/FP8/NVFP4
Ignores tensor-parallel divisibility constraints on group size
evidence_required: Server startup log line naming the selected quantization backend/kernel
Nsight Systems or nsys kernel trace confirming a fused quantized GEMM and no standalone dequant kernel
Per-layer GEMM timing before/after
Device compute capability from nvidia-smi or torch.cuda.get_device_capability

source_user: Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Mechanism (accuracy side, which bounds the latency win you are allowed to keep). Quantization error is dominated by outliers, not by average magnitude. Transformer activations develop a small number of channels with magnitudes 10-100x the rest, concentrated in later layers and in the down-projection input. With per-tensor scaling, one such channel forces a large scale, which collapses the effective resolution of every other channel in that tensor. The standard mitigations are mechanically different: per-channel or group-wise scaling (finer scales, more metadata), SmoothQuant (algebraically migrate activation range into the weights before quantizing both), GPTQ/AWQ (choose weight rounding using calibration-set second-order or salience information rather than nearest-rounding), and keeping a small outlier fraction in FP16.

Calibration is a real dependency: GPTQ/AWQ need a calibration corpus, and if that corpus is off-distribution from production traffic the damage appears specifically on production-like inputs, not on the benchmark.

Boundary condition. Weight-only INT4 is usually safe for accuracy because weight distributions are well behaved; activation quantization (W8A8, FP8 activations) is where outliers bite, and long-context or multilingual traffic degrades first. Perplexity is a poor detector here: a build can lose <0.1 perplexity and still lose several points on structured output, tool-call JSON validity, or long-context retrieval, because those depend on low-probability token discrimination.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: W4A16 with group-128 AWQ loses <=1 point absolute on the held-out task suite while W8A8 per-tensor loses >=2 points on the same suite. Gate: block promotion on any regression in tool-call schema validity or long-context retrieval, regardless of perplexity, and keep the BF16 checkpoint hot for immediate rollback.
risks: Source names calibration and outliers but explains neither the mechanism nor which mitigation addresses which failure
Perplexity-only evaluation hides structured-output and long-context regressions
Calibration-set distribution shift can move the failure into production-only traffic
evidence_required: Per-layer activation magnitude histogram identifying outlier channels
Held-out eval covering tool-call/JSON validity and long-context retrieval, not just perplexity
Documented calibration corpus and its overlap with production traffic distribution
Rollback path to the BF16 checkpoint

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan. Step 0, freeze the comparison: identical model revision, identical server version and flags except the quantization scheme, identical max_model_len, identical scheduler settings, pinned clocks (nvidia-smi -lgc) to remove DVFS drift, and a fixed random seed for request generation. Record device compute capability and driver/CUDA versions.

Step 1, define the SLO first, then measure under it. Report p50 and p99 for TTFT and TPOT at fixed input/output token lengths, and report throughput only as goodput: tokens/s among requests that met the SLO. Peak tokens/s without an SLO is not a decision-grade number.

Step 2, sweep concurrency (1, 4, 16, 64, 128) rather than reporting one point, because the quantized and baseline curves cross. Use a load generator with a fixed arrival process; discard the first 60 s as warmup so autotuning and CUDA graph capture do not contaminate results. Run 3 repetitions and report the spread, not a single run.

Step 3, confirm the mechanism, do not infer it. Check the server log for the selected quantization kernel, and take an nsys/ncu sample to confirm dram bytes per decode step actually fell. If traffic did not fall, any observed speedup came from something else and the experiment is invalid.

Step 4, quality gate in the same harness: held-out task accuracy, tool-call schema validity, long-context retrieval.

Mechanism being tested: reduced weight traffic lowers the bandwidth-bound TPOT floor and frees HBM for KV blocks.

Boundary condition. This plan is only valid while the benchmark's input/output length distribution matches production. A benchmark with 128-token outputs is dominated by prefill and will understate a decode-side win; one with 4k-token outputs will overstate it. Bind the length distribution to sampled production traces.

Gate: adopt only if SLO-constrained goodput improves >=20% and no quality metric regresses beyond the agreed threshold; otherwise roll back to the BF16 build.
risks: Source gives no plan at all, only a statement that things 'must be measured'
Single-concurrency benchmarks hide the crossover where quantization loses
Unpinned clocks and no warmup discard make results irreproducible
Benchmark length distribution mismatched to production biases the conclusion
evidence_required: Concurrency sweep with p50/p99 TTFT and TPOT plus SLO-constrained goodput, 3 repetitions
Server log naming the quantization backend actually used
ncu/nsys evidence that DRAM bytes per decode step decreased
Production-sampled input/output length distribution
Held-out accuracy, tool-call validity, long-context retrieval results

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan, memory-capacity framing. The question 'does quantization help' has two separable answers: does it lower per-token latency, and does it raise the concurrency ceiling. This plan isolates the second.

Step 1, measure the static budget: total HBM, weight bytes after quantization (including scale/zero-point metadata, which is not free), CUDA graph and activation workspace, and the residual left for KV. Get this from server startup logs or torch.cuda.memory_allocated at steady state, not from a paper formula.

Step 2, compute and then verify KV bytes per token: 2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes. Verify by admitting sequences until the scheduler reports the cache full, and compare the observed sequence count against the predicted one. A gap means workspace or fragmentation is larger than assumed.

Step 3, run a capacity sweep at fixed context length (2k, 8k, 32k) and record: max admitted concurrent sequences, preemption/recompute counts, and SLO-constrained goodput. The quantization win shows up as a higher admitted count at equal p99.

Step 4, separate the KV-quantization variable from the weight-quantization variable; changing both at once makes the result uninterpretable.

Mechanism: weight bytes freed convert one-for-one into KV blocks, and KV blocks set the concurrency ceiling under paged attention.

Boundary condition. The conversion stops helping once decode is no longer KV-capacity limited (compute bound at high batch, or bound by CPU-side scheduling and detokenization). At that point extra KV capacity raises queueing latency instead of goodput, and preemption counts stay at zero while p99 still climbs, which is the signature to look for.

Gate: accept only if admitted concurrency rises >=1.5x at 8k context with p99 TTFT inside SLO and zero increase in preemption-driven recomputation; otherwise revert.
risks: Source provides no measurement procedure and no separation of latency from capacity effects
Changing weight quantization and KV quantization together makes results uninterpretable
Predicted KV capacity often overstates reality due to workspace and fragmentation
evidence_required: Measured HBM breakdown at steady state from the running server
Predicted vs observed max concurrent sequences at 2k/8k/32k context
Scheduler preemption and recompute counters
SLO-constrained goodput per configuration

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan, quality-validation framing. Latency numbers are only usable if the quantized build is still correct, so the quality arm must run in the same harness and on the same checkpoint artifact that serves traffic.

Step 1, hash-pin the artifact: record the checkpoint sha256, quantization scheme, group size, calibration corpus identity and size. A quality result that cannot be tied to a hash is not evidence.

Step 2, build a tiered eval. Tier A, cheap regression signal: perplexity on held-out in-domain text (use it only as a smoke test, never as the gate). Tier B, task accuracy on a held-out set that was not used for calibration. Tier C, failure-mode probes that quantization is known to break first: structured/tool-call output schema validity, long-context retrieval at the max supported length, multilingual or rare-token inputs, and numeric/code exactness.

Step 3, control for sampling noise: fix temperature and seed, run each item multiple times if sampling is stochastic, and report confidence intervals. A 1-point difference from a single greedy pass over 200 items is inside noise.

Step 4, compare against the BF16 baseline run on the same day with the same harness version, not against a historical number.

Mechanism: quantization error concentrates in outlier channels and degrades low-probability token discrimination, which is exactly what structured output and long-context retrieval depend on.

Boundary condition. Calibration-set leakage invalidates the whole arm: if the eval set overlaps the calibration corpus, accuracy is inflated in a way that will not reproduce in production. Enforce and document disjointness.

Gate: promote only if Tier B is within the agreed absolute threshold and Tier C shows no regression in schema validity or long-context retrieval; keep the BF16 checkpoint loadable for immediate rollback.
risks: Source names 'accuracy' and 'calibration' without specifying an eval design or a gate
Perplexity-as-gate hides structured-output and long-context regressions
Calibration/eval overlap silently inflates results
Single-pass small-N evals report differences inside noise
evidence_required: Checkpoint sha256 and quantization scheme metadata
Documented disjointness between calibration corpus and eval set
Tiered eval results with confidence intervals against a same-day BF16 baseline
Tool-call schema validity and long-context retrieval scores

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan, mechanism-attribution framing. The failure mode of most quantization benchmarks is that the speedup is real but the stated cause is wrong, which makes the result non-transferable to the next model or GPU.

Step 1, form the hypothesis numerically before running anything: predicted TPOT floor = weight_bytes / HBM_bandwidth. Write down the predicted BF16 and quantized floors and the predicted ratio. Now the experiment can fail.

Step 2, measure single-stream TPOT for both builds. If the measured ratio is far below the predicted ratio, the kernel is not bandwidth bound (dequant overhead, or a fallback path). If it is far above, something else changed: CUDA graphs, a different attention backend, different max_num_seqs, or chunked prefill. Diff the effective server config, not the intended one.

Step 3, confirm with counters rather than inference: ncu dram__bytes_read.sum per decode step, and achieved occupancy / SM utilization from nsys. Bandwidth-bound decode should show high DRAM throughput and modest SM utilization; the quantized build should show materially fewer bytes.

Step 4, only after attribution holds, run the concurrency sweep and the quality arm.

Mechanism under test: fewer weight bytes per decode step lowers the bandwidth-bound floor.

Boundary condition. Attribution breaks when more than one variable moved. Quantized checkpoints frequently ship with a different attention backend or different default max_num_batched_tokens; that alone can produce a double-digit throughput swing unrelated to precision. Enforce one-variable-at-a-time and dump the resolved runtime config for both arms.

Gate: if the measured speedup cannot be attributed to a measured reduction in DRAM traffic, do not claim a quantization win; report it as an unexplained configuration effect and re-run controlled.
risks: Source offers no attribution step, so a config-driven speedup can be misreported as a quantization win
Quantized checkpoints often change attention backend or batching defaults simultaneously
Without a pre-registered prediction the experiment cannot be falsified
evidence_required: Pre-registered predicted TPOT floors and ratio from bandwidth arithmetic
Measured single-stream TPOT for both arms
ncu dram__bytes_read per decode step for both arms
Diff of resolved runtime configuration between arms

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan, production-rollout framing. Offline benchmarks decide whether a quantized build is a candidate; only a controlled rollout decides whether it helps the serving workload.

Step 1, replay real traffic: sample production request traces (input length, output length, arrival timestamps, tool-call fraction) and replay them against both builds. Synthetic fixed-length load will systematically misrank the two arms because the prefill/decode ratio differs.

Step 2, canary at low traffic share behind identical routing, with per-arm dashboards for p50/p99 TTFT, p99 TPOT, goodput, error rate, preemption rate, GPU memory headroom, and any downstream quality signal available online (schema-validity rate of tool calls, retry rate, human thumbs-down).

Step 3, pre-declare the decision rule and the observation window before starting, including the minimum number of requests needed for p99 to be stable. p99 on a few thousand requests is not stable.

Step 4, keep the BF16 deployment warm and the rollback a single routing change; do not free its GPU capacity during the canary.

Mechanism: the quantized build lowers per-token bandwidth cost and raises KV capacity, which should show up as higher SLO-constrained goodput at equal or better p99.

Boundary condition. The rollout is only informative if traffic mix is stationary across the window. A diurnal shift in output-length distribution can move goodput more than the precision change does, so run both arms concurrently under the same traffic rather than sequentially in time.

Gate and rollback: promote only if goodput improves beyond the pre-declared margin with no p99 SLO violation and no rise in tool-call schema failures or retries; roll back immediately on any error-rate or quality-signal regression, and record the exact checkpoint hash and server config of both arms in the experiment log.
risks: Source gives no rollout or rollback procedure for a change that alters model outputs in production
Synthetic fixed-length load misranks builds relative to real traffic
Sequential A/B across time confounds diurnal traffic shifts with the precision change
Freeing the baseline deployment removes the rollback path
evidence_required: Production trace sample with input/output length and arrival distributions
Concurrent canary metrics per arm: p50/p99 TTFT, p99 TPOT, goodput, error rate, preemption rate
Pre-declared decision rule and minimum request count for p99 stability
Online quality signals such as tool-call schema validity and retry rate
Checkpoint hashes and resolved configs for both arms

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about quantization? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions that must be stated before any quantization performance claim. (1) Hardware: exact GPU model, compute capability, HBM capacity and bandwidth, NVLink/PCIe topology, and clock policy (pinned or not). An INT4 or FP8 claim is arch-specific: FP8 tensor cores start at Hopper SM90, so on Ampere A30 an FP8 claim is about storage, not compute. (2) Model identity: parameter count, layer/head/head_dim geometry, GQA kv_heads, and checkpoint hash. (3) Quantization scheme, stated in full: which tensors are quantized (weights only, or weights and activations, or KV too), bit width, granularity (per-tensor / per-channel / group size), and the calibration method and corpus. 'INT4' alone is not a specification. (4) Runtime: server and kernel backend actually selected, tensor-parallel degree, attention backend, chunked prefill on/off, CUDA graph on/off, max_num_seqs and max_model_len. (5) Workload: input and output token length distributions, concurrency, and arrival process. (6) Metric definition: which percentile, TTFT vs TPOT vs end-to-end, and whether throughput is peak or SLO-constrained goodput. (7) Measurement hygiene: warmup discarded, repetition count, variance reported. (8) Which numbers are measured on this system versus estimated from bandwidth arithmetic or quoted from a vendor.

Mechanism, stated so the claim is checkable: the expected win is reduced weight/KV bytes moved per decode step against a fixed HBM bandwidth, plus freed capacity converting into KV blocks and higher admitted concurrency.

Boundary condition. The claim is void outside the measured regime. A speedup measured at concurrency 1 with 512-token outputs does not transfer to concurrency 64 with 128-token outputs, where the workload is compute and prefill dominated and the same build can be slower. State the regime with every number.

Gate: if any of the above is unknown, report the result as provisional and non-transferable rather than as a performance claim, and keep the baseline checkpoint available for rollback.
risks: Source does not enumerate any assumption, so claims built on it are non-reproducible
Bit width alone underspecifies a quantization scheme (granularity and calibration omitted)
Omitting the measured regime lets a narrow result be generalized incorrectly
Measured vs estimated vs vendor-quoted numbers get conflated
evidence_required: Hardware inventory: GPU model, compute capability, HBM bandwidth, topology, clock policy
Checkpoint hash and full quantization scheme specification
Resolved runtime configuration dump from the running server
Workload length distribution and concurrency used for the measurement
Explicit labeling of each number as measured, estimated, or vendor-quoted
